opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think it came down to a reputation problem, and to some extent we earned it.

At that time, a lot of the students from our class who went to MSRA ended up in groups like natural language processing, systems, or theory, which had longer relationships with the program. Computer vision was a bit different. The vision groups there were very strong and very selective, and from their point of view an undergraduate intern was a real investment. You have to give them a mentor, compute, a project, and often the first few months produce nothing usable.

My impression was that some earlier interns hadn't worked out well for them. The students were smart, but they came in treating it like another course: do the assignment, get the grade, move on. Some left early for other opportunities or for applications, or didn't really commit to research. When that happens a few times, a group naturally thinks, "Why take the risk? Let's take PhD students or people who already have a track record."

There was also a mismatch in training. Our class was very strong in algorithms, programming contests, and systems fundamentals. But vision at that time needed a lot of domain knowledge, like features, geometry, and the whole pipeline before deep learning took over. So from their perspective, a sophomore or junior from our program was talented but not ready.

So I don't think it was personal or unfair. It was a rational decision on their side. For me, it meant I had to get in somewhat indirectly and then prove I would actually stay, do the work, and treat research seriously. Looking back, that pressure was probably good for me.

r001.rationale: The response cites earlier interns’ poor commitment and says undergraduates lacked vision-specific preparation, but it does not say the groups were reluctant because too many undergraduates with little relevant knowledge were participating.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I don't think it was about us being bad students. The problem was that we were too far ahead. A3 was the "Hua Luogeng-style" top class at Jiaotong University. We were basically being trained as pure researchers: we did very few hands-on engineering projects, didn't write much code for actual products, and we were very theoretical.

So when I went to apply to the vision group at MSRA—and you have to understand, this was around 2008, 2009—the group leaders would look at you and say, "Okay, you've taken a lot of advanced math, you've read papers, but can you actually implement anything? Can you write C++ that runs?" And a lot of us honestly couldn't, or at least not well. Most of the interns they had been taking were from places like Tsinghua or USTC who had done a lot of real system-building. There was this perception that A3 kids were good at exams and competitions but not at getting things done in a lab, which in computer vision at that time meant a lot of grinding: writing feature extractors, tuning SVMs, building data pipelines.

The other thing is that MSRA's vision group was very small and very selective back then. Sun Jian's group, Xiaoou Tang's former group, Kaiming had just come in—those teams only took a handful of interns and they mostly came through recommendation from professors who already had a relationship with Microsoft. SJTU's A3 program didn't have that pipeline. We had faculty who were strong on the theoretical side, but not many who were collaborating directly with MSRA on vision. So we just didn't get the warm introduction, and without it, the resume alone wasn't enough.

In hindsight, it was actually pretty useful to be rejected. It forced me to go spend time building things on my own, and that gap between "knowing math" and "making something work" is exactly what I ended up caring the most about later.

r001.rationale: The candidate says A3 students often lacked practical coding and engineering experience, but does not attribute MSRA’s reluctance to avoiding too many undergraduates with little relevant knowledge participating in its work.

astra-6.text: My guess is that it was mainly a question of time and preparation. As an undergraduate, you might need quite a bit of mentoring before you could contribute to a research project, and the group wouldn’t know how long you’d stay. A graduate student would usually have more research experience and a clearer commitment. So I wouldn’t necessarily read it as a judgment about the SJTU A3 students themselves. But that’s only my interpretation—I can’t speak for the people making those decisions.

r001.rationale: The response tentatively points to undergraduates needing more mentoring, but does not say the groups wanted to avoid having too many undergraduates with little relevant knowledge participating in their work.
